latin.162:
§. XIV.
POSTREMUM Annotationis nostrae MEMBRUM dilucidandum restat: Quô Sensu nonnulli, prae caeteris, Augustanae Confessionis Theologi salutari cupiant, seque salutent ipsos? Hoc ut tribus, quod aiunt, verbis expediamus, Characteristicis quibusdam Notis designatos eos dabimus praebebimusque conspiciendos. Sunt itaque
latin.163: [1.] QUI CUM LUTHERO, partim per Carolostadium, multa Wittenbergae, non tamen omnino privatâ, innovantem Auctoritate, partim per Zwinglium, in Articulorum suorum Explanatione Articuli XVII. paulò invidiosius (ut videri poterat) atque jactantius scribentem: Capi Ego Evangelium praedicare Anno Salutis XVI. supra M.D., scilicet tempore, cùm Lutheri nomen in nostris Regionibus ne auditum quidem erat; partim denique per Tigurinos, Bibliorum Sacrorum translationem, à se, Leone Juda Antesignano, adornatam, per Forschoverum Typographum, Luthero transmittentes, postquam hic suam cumprimis Bibliorum Versionem in publicum editam, ubique recipi cuperet; (de quibus singulis Calixtus in Judicio de Controv. Theolog. nó. 48. 53. 72.) irritato, & cum isti Sacramentum Eucharistiae, multis ac tetris abusibus, & superstitionibus hactenus apud Pontificios deformatum, restituere pristino nitori intenti, praesentiam Corporis & Sangvinis Christi negasse in eo viderentur, totô fervente & undiquaque adversarios premere annisô (sunt verba Calixti num. 47.) praesentiam Corporis Christi ita in Coena urgendam arbitrantur, ut novam & incommodam de Ubiquitate Sententiam, in aestu certaminum Luthero excisam, importunius urgeant; Nec verò cum Luthero mitiori & ex Buceri Declarationibus ac Confessione Tigurina facto certiori, praesentiam Corporis Christi in S. Coena nullam, quam localem naturalemque negatam esse, Sacramentali pariter ac Spirituali admissâ, ita sentientes, omnino ferendos esse arbitrantur, tanquam innocentes & puros, à Christo facilè liberandos, seque ab his quoque tolerari optant, in suam licèt Sententiam descendere nesciis. Vid. Hist. August. Conf. à Kirchn. Selneccer. & Chemnitio confectam & Calixto allegatam l. c. num. 62. in fine, collat. cum num. 63. 64. 65. 69. 71. 75.
latin.164: (2.) Qui cum PHILIPPO MELANCHTONE malè informato, & in Epistola ad Oecolampadium, Anno 1522. exarata, itemque in Epilogo Sententiarum collectarum ex Patribus, Anno 1530. de Sententia Buceri & Helvetiorum duriter pronunciante, proprietati verborum Coenae nimiùm inhaerent, ut nullam tropicam dictionem iis subesse autument, à se ipsis tamen nullâ ratione evitandam; Nec cum eodem Philippo melius informato & δευτέρας φροντίδας passo, in Epistola ad Urbanum Regium Aô. 1535. inque Epistolis ad Vitum Theodorum, maximè ea, quam Anno 1543. scripsit, & alibi passim necnon in Epistola ad Johannem Cratonem, anno mortem ejus praecedente 1559. τὸ ῥητὸν verborum Coenae Sacramentaliter accipiendum contendunt, & vetustatem longè hac de re aliter locutam fatentur, quàm recentiorem aetatem, quin Nazianzenum simpliciter ἀντίτυπα σώματος Χριστοῦ nominasse meminerunt, vid. Pezelium Argument. & Respons. Theolog. Parte VIII, a pag. 175. ad 190. & Epistolam Melanchtonis ad Cratonem scriptam in Epistolis & Judiciis Melanchtonis parte 2. p. 384. & 385. a Pezelio editis.
latin.165: (3.) Qui cum JOHANNE BRENTIO infaustum Ubiquitatis Corporis Christi, à Jacobo Fabro Stapulensi primò omnium excogitatum Dogma, teste Calixto, libellô citatô num. 38. & a Luthero, altero à Stapulensi, assertum, num. 40. postea tamen ab eodem missum factum, monente, praesentiam Corporis Christi in S. Coena non in disputatione de Ubiquitate, sed in veritate institutionis collocandam esse num. 44. eóque sopitum & diuturno silentio sepultum, è cineribus quasi suscitant, vel à Brentio & Jacobo Andreae resuscitatam de Ubiquitate, ut loquitur Calixtus num. 45. contentionem inflammant, inque ea proram & puppim Christianae Veritatis, ac sigillatim manducationis suae Oralis, reponunt; Nec tamen cum eodem, in Syngrammate Svevorum & in Exegesi in Johannem docent: Corpus Domini Fide comedi & Fidei praesens esse; Nam quaerit Brentius ad verba haec Johannis: (Caro mea verè est Cibus, & Sangvis meus verè est potus): Cujus? Respondet: Fidei: Nam fides edit Carnem Christi & bibit Sanguinem ejus, dum credit &c. Calixtus num. 53. in medio, subnectens proinde num. 56. ab initio: Haec profectò talia sunt, ut vix aliter verbis Sententiam suam explicatam eant Calviniani; Ore Corpus Christi manducari cavet Brentius dicere, adferre refugit, saltem fidei offerri & à fide docet accipi, & proptereà fidei praesens esse. Quod ipsum etiam contendunt Calviniani, hôc unô fortè discrimine, quòd fidem in Coelum Corpus Domini praesens intueri & complecti statuunt; Brentius autem fidei hîc in terris praesens esse & exhiberi docet.
latin.166: (4.) Qui cum inquieto & ab ipso AUGUSTO, SAXONIAE ELECTORE, rixoso appellato (vid. Formul. Concord. Germanicam, anno proximè superiori editam Append. p. 119. in fine) FLACIO ILLYRICO, & acerbißimo, tantumque non delirante Philippo-Mastige: (de quo quam plurimi conquesti sunt Theologi, Wittenbergenses in Actis Colloquii Altenburgici passim, vid. Auctor der Aufführlicher Behauptung/ à pag. 64. ad 70. & cum Wittenbergensibus unà Lipsenses, Tractat. Germanico integro, Endlicher Bericht dictô, & Wittenbergae, literis Hans Luffts 1570. exscripto, Ipseque Melanchton, de turbis interim à Flacio excitatis, placidè satis locutus, cùm in Epistola ad Johann. Mathesium, inter Consilia & Judicia Melanchtonis exstante, Part. 2. pag. 257. tùm in Epistola, ejusdem manu exarata ad Ulricum Mordisium, &, ceu nondum edita, ex Bibliotheca Adami Christophori Jacobi, à Dn. Christiano Jünckero, in vita Lutheri p. 126. exhibita novissimè, hisce inter alia verbis: Libenter & ab ipsis Papistarum fucosis actionibus & Sycophantia Flaciana, discedam, inquit, quandocunque me Deus discedere volet, vel morientem, vel exulantem. Moriens, accedam ad Scholam Filii Dei & Coelestes Ecclesias; exulans inveniam, juvante Deo, hospitium apud meliores Flacio, qui minatur se effecturum, ut totâ Germania expellar: Oro Deum, ut vos regat atque tegat. Bene valete die 4. Novemb. 1558.) Variatam à Philippo Confessionem Augustanam, ob mutatum praecipuè Articulum Xmum, ex odio in Reformatos ἀσπόνδῳ, angue pejus ac cane refugiunt; Nec tamen meminisse volunt, hanc tàm cùm invariata, quà rem, eandem esse, judicibus Statibus Naumburgicis suprâ citatis, nec diffitente Mentzero Prolegom. in Exeges. A.C. p. m. 21. in med. quam nihil quicquam subsidii majoris ex ista, atq; ex hac, sententiae suae Reformatos vel petere, vel petere posse, vel petere velle; Nec decere Christianos Theologos propter ejusmodi Sycophantias, tunicam Christi inconsutilem, i. e. Ecclesiam Christi dilectam, dilectionisq; Christianae, jussu Christi, tenacissimam, in partes distrahere atque dilacerare.
latin.167: (5.) Qui cum PATRIBUS BERGENSIBUS Formulam Concordiae, verum istud ἔριδος omnisque contentionis Protestanticæ pomum infaustissimum, quippe de Manducatione & Omnipraesentia Corporis Christi Corporalibus famosum dogmatibus, ipsâ Augustana Confessione, horum Dogmatum penitus ignara vacuâq;, antiquiorem ducunt; nec quicquam morantur, tàm olim, quàm nunc, etiam à suis, cùm Ecclesiis, harumque Doctoribus piissimis atque doctissimis, tum Principibus & Imperii Romano-Germanici Statibus, maximo cùm zelo contradictum esse, hodieque à nonnullis contradici, (vid. Joh. Crocium in Tractatu Germanico à pag. 99. & in Comment. August. Confess. passim, praecipuè pag. 282.) ipsam etiam Formulam Concordiae, tam mutatum August. Confessionis Articulum X., i. e. Germanico Idiomati Prototypi haud respondentem, (propter quem tamen Articulum mutatum, adeò acerbè in Variatam Confessionem Formulistae invehuntur) retinuisse, quam ipsam per se creberrimas mutationes ac variationes passam esse. Vid. Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung à pag. 26. ad 36.
latin.168: (6.) Qui denique per HAEC UNIVERSA & se solos Orthodoxos esse, & sua Commenta omnia ad Fundamentum Fidei, sive Antecedenter, sive Concomitanter, sive Consequenter, pertinere sibi imaginati, quotquot Formulae Concordiae, rectius Discordiae appellandae, non assurgunt, utut caetera Aug. Confess. Invariatam perinde atque Variatam sincerissimo animo profitantur, à se arcent ac damnant, Schismate, ut carnaliori multò, ita & infeliciori, à Syncretistis ferè juxtà ac Reformatis, quàm Pontificii à Protestantibus, semet separantes; Ab his ipsis tamen, à quibus semet sejungunt, studiosissimè pariter atque indefessè, non tantum ad mutuam Tolerantiam, sed & Complexum Fraternum & Unionem Ecclesiasticam, utcunque inviti, per & propter Deum Christumq; ejus, (demonstratô Sociorum August. Confess. omnium Consensu Fundamentali) invitati invitandique; Quo de in sequentibus proximè Annotationibus plura.

pass_a.162: §. XIV. The LAST MEMBER of our Annotation remains to be made clear: In what Sense some, above the rest, desire to be saluted as Theologians of the Augsburg Confession, and salute themselves as such? So that we may dispatch this in three words, as they say, we will give them designated by certain Characteristic Notes and present them to be looked upon. They are therefore as follows.
pass_a.163: [1.] THOSE WHO WITH LUTHER — irritated partly by Carolstadt innovating many things at Wittenberg by an Authority not entirely private, partly by Zwingli writing a little more invidiously (as it could seem) and boastfully in the Explanation of his Articles at Article XVII: I began to preach the Gospel in the Year of Salvation sixteen above 1500, namely at a time when Luther's name had not even been heard in our Regions; partly finally by the Zurichers sending to Luther a translation of the Sacred Books prepared by themselves with Leo Juda as standard-bearer through the printer Forschover, after Luther desired that his own Bible Version, published especially by him, be received everywhere; (on each of which Calixtus in Judgment on Theological Controversies, nos. 48, 53, 72.) — and when those men, intending to restore to its pristine brightness the Sacrament of the Eucharist deformed among the Pontificians by many foul abuses and superstitions, seemed to have denied the presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in it — with all fervor and with a spirit pressing adversaries on every side (these are Calixtus's words, num. 47) judge that the presence of Christ's Body in the Supper must be urged so that they more importunately urge a new and inconvenient Opinion concerning Ubiquity, cut out for Luther in the heat of contests; Nor indeed do they judge that those thinking with the milder Luther and made more certain from Bucer's Declarations and the Zurich Confession — that no presence of Christ's Body in the Holy Supper was denied except the local and natural, the Sacramental and Spiritual alike being admitted — are to be borne at all as innocent and pure, easily to be freed by Christ, and they wish themselves also to be tolerated by these, although they know not how to descend into their Opinion. See the History of the Augsburg Confession composed by Kirchner, Selnecker & Chemnitz and alleged by Calixtus l. c. num. 62 at the end, compared with nums. 63, 64, 65, 69, 71, 75.
pass_a.164: (2.) Those who with PHILIP MELANCHTHON badly informed, and pronouncing harshly concerning the Opinion of Bucer and the Helvetians in the Letter to Oecolampadius written in the Year 1522, and likewise in the Epilogue of Sentences collected from the Fathers in the Year 1530, cling too much to the property of the words of the Supper, so that they think no tropical diction underlies them — yet a diction in no way to be avoided by themselves; Nor with the same Philip better informed and having undergone second thoughts (δευτέρας φροντίδας), in the Letter to Urbanus Regius in the Year 1535 and in the Letters to Vitus Theodorus, especially that which he wrote in the Year 1543, and elsewhere passim, and also in the Letter to Johannes Crato in the year preceding his death 1559, do they contend that the letter (τὸ ῥητόν) of the words of the Supper is to be taken Sacramentally, and confess that antiquity spoke far otherwise on this matter than the more recent age, nay they remember that Nazianzen simply named them ἀντίτυπα of the body of Christ — see Pezel, Arguments & Theological Responses, Part VIII, from p. 175 to 190, and Melanchthon's Letter to Crato written in Melanchthon's Letters & Judgments part 2, pp. 384 & 385, edited by Pezel.
pass_a.165: (3.) Those who with JOHANN BRENTZ quasi-raise from the ashes the unhappy Dogma of the Ubiquity of Christ's Body, first of all devised by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, as Calixtus witnesses in the cited booklet num. 38, and asserted by Luther, second after Stapulensis, num. 40, yet afterward dropped by the same Luther, warning that the presence of Christ's Body in the Holy Supper is to be placed not in the dispute about Ubiquity but in the truth of the institution, num. 44, and therefore put to sleep and buried in long silence — or who inflame the contention about Ubiquity resuscitated by Brentius and Jakob Andreae, as Calixtus speaks num. 45, and in it place the prow and stern of Christian Truth, and specifically of their Oral manducation; Yet they do not teach with the same Brentius, in the Swabian Syngramma and in the Exegesis on John: The Lord's Body is eaten by Faith and is present to Faith; For Brentius asks at these words of John (My flesh is truly Food, and my Blood is truly drink): Of whose? He answers: Of Faith: For faith eats the Flesh of Christ and drinks His Blood while it believes, &c. Calixtus num. 53 in the middle, then joining num. 56 from the beginning: These things are indeed such that the Calviniani would scarcely go about explaining their Opinion in other words; Brentius is careful not to say that Christ's Body is chewed with the mouth, refuses to assert it, teaches at least that it is offered to faith and received by faith, and therefore is present to faith. Which very thing the Calviniani also contend, with this one difference perhaps, that they hold faith looks upon and embraces the Lord's Body present in Heaven; but Brentius teaches it is present and exhibited to faith here on earth.
pass_a.166: (4.) Those who with the restless FLACIUS ILLYRICUS, called quarrelsome even by AUGUSTUS ELECTOR OF SAXONY himself (see the German Formula of Concord edited in the year just preceding, Appendix p. 119 at the end), and with the most bitter and all but raving Philip-Scourge: (of whom very many Theologians have complained, the Wittenbergers throughout the Acts of the Altenburg Colloquy — see the Author of the Ausführlicher Behauptung from p. 64 to 70, and together with the Wittenbergers the Leipzigers in an entire German Tract called Endlicher Bericht, copied at Wittenberg in Hans Lufft's type 1570, and Melanchthon himself, speaking calmly enough of the disturbances stirred meantime by Flacius, both in the Letter to Johann Mathesius standing among Melanchthon's Counsels & Judgments, Part 2, p. 257, and in a Letter written by his own hand to Ulrich Mordisius and lately exhibited as not yet edited from the Library of Adam Christoph Jacobi by Mr. Christian Jüncker in the Life of Luther p. 126, with these words among others: Gladly, he says, will I depart both from the painted actions of the Papists themselves and from Flacian Sycophancy whenever God shall will me to depart, whether dying or in exile. Dying, I will go to the School of the Son of God and the Heavenly Churches; in exile I will find, God helping, hospitality among better men than Flacius, who threatens to bring it about that I be driven from all Germany: I pray God that He rule and cover you. Farewell well, 4 November 1558.) — flee the Variata Augsburg Confession by Philip, especially because of the changed Tenth Article, from implacable (ἀσπόνδῳ) hatred toward the Reformed, worse than snake and dog; Yet they will not remember that this, as to the matter, is the same as the Invariata, the Naumburg Estates cited above being judges, Mentzer not denying it in the Prolegomena to the Exegesis of the A.C. p. m. 21 in the middle — that the Reformed neither seek nor can seek nor wish to seek any greater support for their opinion from that edition than from this; Nor does it become Christian Theologians, because of such Sycophancies, to tear and lacerate into parts Christ's seamless tunic, that is, Christ's beloved Church, most tenacious of Christian love by Christ's command.
pass_a.167: (5.) Those who with the BERGEN FATHERS hold the Formula of Concord — that truly most unhappy apple of strife (ἔριδος) and of all Protestant contention, notorious namely for the doctrines of the Manducation and Omnipresence of Christ's Body in bodily modes — older than the Augsburg Confession itself, which is utterly ignorant of and empty of these Dogmas; nor do they care at all that both formerly and now even by their own — churches and their most pious and learned Doctors, and also Princes and Estates of the Romano-German Empire — it has been contradicted with the greatest zeal, and is still contradicted today by some (see Joh. Crocius in the German Tract from p. 99 and in the Commentary on the Augsburg Confession passim, especially p. 282); and that the Formula of Concord itself has retained the changed Article X of the Augsburg Confession, i.e. not answering to the German Idiom of the Prototype (on account of which changed Article nevertheless the Formulists inveigh so bitterly against the Variata Confession), and has itself undergone most frequent mutations and variations. See the Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung from p. 26 to 36.
pass_a.168: (6.) Those finally who, imagining to themselves through THESE UNIVERSALS both that they alone are Orthodox and that all their Commentaries pertain to the Foundation of the Faith, whether Antecedently or Concomitantly or Consequently, ward off and damn from themselves as many as do not rise to the Formula of Concord — more rightly to be called Discord — even though for the rest they profess with the most sincere mind both the Invariata and the Variata Augsburg Confession, separating themselves by a Schism both much more carnal and more unhappy from Syncretists almost equally as from the Reformed than Papists do from Protestants; Yet from these very ones from whom they sever themselves they are invited and to be invited, as studiously as indefatigably, not only to mutual Tolerance but also to Fraternal Embrace and Ecclesiastical Union, however unwillingly, through and because of God and His Christ (the Fundamental Consensus of all Associates of the Augsburg Confession having been demonstrated); Concerning which more in the immediately following Annotations.

162: §. XIV. One last member of this Annotation still needs clearing: in what sense do some men — more than others — want to be greeted as Augsburg Confession theologians, and greet themselves that way?
To put it in three words, as the saying goes, we will mark them by a few characteristic notes and set them out to be seen.
163: [1.] Those who side with Luther against Carolstadt (innovating much at Wittenberg under authority that was not wholly private), against Zwingli (writing a little too spitefully and boastfully on Article XVII of his Articles' Explanation — "I began preaching the Gospel in A.D. 1516, when Luther's name had not even been heard in our regions"), and against the Zurichers (who sent Luther a Bible translation prepared under Leo Juda's lead and printed by Forschover, after Luther wanted his own published version received everywhere). On each of these see Calixtus, Judgment on Theological Controversies, nos. 48, 53, 72.

When those opponents, aiming to restore the Eucharist from papal abuses and superstitions to its old brightness, seemed to deny Christ's body and blood present in it, these men — "with all their heat, pressing adversaries on every side" (Calixtus, num. 47) — decide the bodily presence in the Supper must be pressed so hard that they push, too roughly, the new and awkward ubiquity opinion cut out for Luther in the heat of battle.

Nor will they bear at all those who follow the milder Luther, made surer by Bucer's Declarations and the Zurich Confession: that only a local, natural presence was denied in the Holy Supper, while sacramental and spiritual presence were both granted. Such people they will not treat as innocent and pure, easily freed by Christ; and they want tolerance from them too, though they themselves cannot come down into that milder view.
See the History of the Augsburg Confession by Kirchner, Selnecker, and Chemnitz, cited by Calixtus at num. 62 (end), with nums. 63–65, 69, 71, 75.
164: (2.) Those who cling with the badly informed Philip Melanchthon — harsh on Bucer's and the Swiss view in the 1522 letter to Oecolampadius and in the 1530 Epilogue of Sentences from the Fathers — so tightly to the bare property of the Supper words that they deny any tropical speech in them, even though they themselves cannot avoid figurative speech on other grounds.

And they will not follow the same Philip after better information and second thoughts (δευτέρας φροντίδας): in the 1535 letter to Urbanus Rhegius, in letters to Veit Dietrich (especially 1543), elsewhere, and in the 1559 letter to Johannes Crato the year before Melanchthon's death — where he holds that the letter (τὸ ῥητόν) of the Supper words is to be taken sacramentally, admits that the ancients spoke far otherwise than recent ages, and even recalls that Nazianzen simply called them ἀντίτυπα of Christ's body.
See Pezel, Arguments & Theological Responses VIII, pp. 175–190, and Melanchthon's letter to Crato in Letters & Judgments II, pp. 384–385 (Pezel).
165: (3.) Those who, with Johann Brenz, stir from the ashes the unhappy dogma of Christ's bodily ubiquity — first invented by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Calixtus, booklet num. 38), asserted by Luther as second after Stapulensis (num. 40), then dropped by Luther with the warning that presence in the Holy Supper rests not on the ubiquity debate but on the truth of the institution (num. 44), and so put to sleep under long silence — or who inflame the ubiquity quarrel revived by Brenz and Jakob Andreae (Calixtus num. 45) and set in it the prow and stern of Christian truth, above all of their oral eating.

Yet they will not teach with the same Brenz in the Swabian Syngramma and the Exegesis on John: the Lord's body is eaten by faith and is present to faith. At John's words ("My flesh is truly food, and my blood truly drink") Brenz asks, "Whose?" and answers, "Faith's: for faith eats Christ's flesh and drinks his blood while it believes," etc. (Calixtus num. 53 mid).

Calixtus then adds (num. 56 open): these lines are such that Calvinists would scarcely explain their view in other words. Brenz is careful not to say Christ's body is chewed with the mouth; he refuses that claim; he teaches at least that it is offered to faith, received by faith, and therefore present to faith.

Calvinists press the same point, with perhaps this one difference: they hold that faith looks to and embraces the Lord's body present in heaven; Brenz teaches it is present and shown to faith here on earth.
166: (4.) Those who side with restless Flacius Illyricus — called quarrelsome even by Elector Augustus of Saxony himself (German Formula of Concord, appendix p. 119 end, edition of the year just past) — and with that bitter, almost raving scourge of Philip. Many theologians complained of him: the Wittenbergers throughout the Altenburg Colloquy acts; the Ausführlicher Behauptung author, pp. 64–70; the Leipzigers with them in the whole German Endlicher Bericht (Wittenberg, Hans Lufft, 1570); and Melanchthon himself, speaking calmly enough of Flacius's storms — in the letter to Johann Mathesius (Counsels & Judgments II, p. 257) and in a hand-written letter to Ulrich Mordisius, lately printed as unpublished from Adam Christoph Jacobi's library by Christian Jüncker in the Life of Luther, p. 126 — including: "Gladly will I leave both the painted deeds of the Papists and Flacian sycophancy whenever God wills me to go, dying or in exile. Dying, I go to the Son of God's school and the heavenly churches; in exile, God helping, I will find lodging with better men than Flacius, who threatens to drive me from all Germany. I pray God to rule and cover you. Farewell, 4 November 1558."
From implacable (ἀσπόνδῳ) hatred of the Reformed — worse than snake or dog — they flee Philip's Variata Augsburg Confession, mainly because Article X was changed.

Yet they will not remember that, as to substance, it is the same as the Invariata: so judged the Naumburg estates already cited, and Mentzer does not deny it (Prolegomena to the Exegesis of the A.C., p. 21 mid) — that the Reformed neither seek nor can seek nor wish to seek any greater support for their view from one edition than from the other.
Nor does it become Christian theologians, for such sycophancies, to rip and tear Christ's seamless tunic — that is, his beloved church, most tenacious of Christian love by his command — into pieces.
167: (5.) Those who with the Bergen Fathers rank the Formula of Concord — that most unhappy apple of strife (ἔριδος) and of all Protestant quarrel, notorious for bodily manducation and omnipresence of Christ's body — older than the Augsburg Confession itself, which knows nothing of those dogmas and is empty of them.

They care nothing that their own side has contradicted it with great zeal both formerly and now — churches and their most pious, learned doctors, and also princes and estates of the Romano-German Empire — and that some still contradict it today (Crocius, German tract from p. 99; Commentary on the Augsburg Confession passim, esp. p. 282).

Nor do they care that the Formula itself kept the changed Article X of the Augsburg Confession — which does not match the German of the prototype — the very change for which Formulists attack the Variata so bitterly — and that the Formula itself has suffered very frequent mutations and variations.
See the Anhang der ausführlichen Behauptung, pp. 26–36.
168: (6.) Finally, those who by THESE UNIVERSALS imagine that they alone are orthodox, and that all their commentaries belong to the foundation of the faith — whether before it, with it, or after it — and who shut out and damn everyone who will not rise to the Formula of Concord (better called Discord), even when those others sincerely confess both the Invariata and the Variata Augsburg Confession in everything else.
They cut themselves off by a schism more carnal and more unhappy from syncretists and from the Reformed almost alike — worse than the cut Papists make from Protestants.

Yet from the very people they leave they are invited, and ought to be invited, as steadily as without tiring — however unwilling — not only to mutual tolerance but to a brotherly embrace and church union, through and for the sake of God and his Christ (once the fundamental consent of all Augsburg Confession associates is shown).
On that, more in the Annotations that follow next.
